title: Varsha Khanna vs M/S Ksbl Securities Ltd on 10 July, 2026
full_text: Varsha Khanna vs M/S Ksbl Securities Ltd on 10 July, 2026 IN THE COURT OF Ms. AASTHA SHARMA, LD. JMFC (N.I. Date of judgment/order 10.07.2026 Date of Institution : 13.11.2019 Date of Reserving Judgment/Order : 29.06.2026 Date of Pronouncement of Judgment/Order : 10.07.2026. ARGUING COUNSELS: Ld. Counsel for the complainant : Sh. Arif Shakeel Ld. Counsel for the Accused no. 2. : Mr. Naman Aggarwal, Mr. Shivang Gupta and Mr. Mukund Sharma. CC No. 41970/2019 Varsha Khanna Versus M/s KSBL Securities Limited Page 3 of 15 Digitally signed by AASTHA SHARMA AASTHA Date: SHARMA 2026.07.10 16:46:40 +0530 JUDGMENT 1. Vide this judgment, this Court shall dispose of the present complaint filed by the complainant Ms. Varsha Khanna (hereinafter referred to as "complainant") against M/s KSBL Securities Limited (hereinafter "accused"), its managing director Mr. Ramesh Chand Arora (hereinafter 'accused number 2') and its director Mr. Tika Ram Khare (hereinafter 'accused number 3') under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 read with Section 142 of Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (hereinafter referred to as " NI Act "). Brief facts of the case: 2. It is the case of the complainant, A. That, the complainant invested Rs. 9,00,000/- with the accused in lieu of a promise of high interest to be paid to her. That, the complainant transferred the abovesaid money to the accused through a cheque and a MoU dated 10.07.2017 was signed between the parties. That, the accused paid interest to her only for a few months and then stopped paying the interest. That, the complainant wrote a letter dated 15.07.2019 regarding termination of the MoU. That, after sending the notice the complainant presented the cheque bearing number 003968 dated 28.08.2019, for an amount of Rs. 9,00,000/-, which is drawn in the name of the accused and is the cheque in question. B. That, on presentation of the aforesaid cheques in question by the complainant with his banker State Bank of India, Lajpat Nagar Branch, New Delhi, CC No. 41970/2019 Varsha Khanna Versus M/s KSBL Securities Limited Page 4 of 15 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2026.07.10 16:46:48 +0530 the cheque was dishonoured with the remarks "Payment stopped by the drawer" vide return memo dated 29.08.2019. C. In these circumstances, the complainant got issued a statutory legal demand notice to the accused through her counsel, dated 25.09.2019, thereby requiring the accused to pay the amount of the aforesaid cheques within a period of 15 days from the receipt of the said notice. The said notice under Sec. 138 of NI Act was sent to the accused persons through Registered AD/Speed Post/Courier at their correct address. That despite service of the above stated notice of demand, the accused has deliberately and willfully failed to comply with the said notice of demand and has failed to pay the amount of the aforesaid cheque within the stipulated period of 15 days from the date of receipt of the said notice. Consequently, this case was filed by the complainant against the accused, which was within the limitation period as laid down u/s 138 , NI Act. 3. In the pre-summoning evidence, the complainant examined himself on affidavit being Ex. CW1/1 and placed on record Copy of MoU dated 06.09.2017 Ex. CW1/A; Letter dated 11.07.2019 Ex. CW1/B; the cheque in question Ex. CW1/C; Copy of the bank return memo dated 03.10.2019 Ex. CW1/D; legal demand notice dated 15.10.2019 Ex. CW1/E; postal receipts Ex. CW1/F (colly); POD and returned envelopes Ex. CW1/G (colly). 4. Upon prima facie consideration of the pre-summoning evidence, the accused and accused number 2 were summoned. Accused number 3 was not summoned. CC No. 41970/2019 Varsha Khanna Versus M/s KSBL Securities Limited Page 5 of 15 Digitally signed by AASTHA SHARMA AASTHA Date: SHARMA 2026.07.10 16:46:54 +0530 5. Upon the appearance of the accused, notice under Section 251 CrPC was served upon him on 05.08.2024 to which he pleaded not guilty. The accused has accepted issuance of cheque in favour of the complainant and also his signatures on the cheque in question. The accused has denied receiving the legal demand notice. The accused has stated that the cheque in question has been misused by the complainant; they were security cheque. 6. Vide separate statement of accused, admissions and denials u/s 294 CrPC was recorded and witnesses 2, 3 and 4 from the list of complainant witnesses were dropped. 7. CW-1 was examined-in-chief, cross-examined and discharged. Thereby, CE was closed. Accordingly, the matter proceeded to the stage of recording the statement of the accused. 8. Statement of accused under Section 313 CrPC read with Section 281 CrPC was recorded on 16.03.2026 wherein the accused opted to lead defence evidence. DW-1 was examined in chief, cross-examined and discharged and therefore, vide order of this court, DE was closed by the order of the court on 06.04.2026. 9. Thereafter, the matter was listed for final arguments. After hearing the final arguments from both sides, the matter was reserved for pronouncement of judgment. 10. It is well settled position of law that to constitute an offence under Section 138 , NI Act, the following ingredients are required to be fulfilled: CC No. 41970/2019 Varsha Khanna Versus M/s KSBL Securities Limited Page 6 of 15 Digitally signed by AASTHA SHARMA AASTHA Date: SHARMA 2026.07.10 16:46:58 +0530 I. drawing of the cheque by a person on an account maintained by him with a banker, II. The cheque was issued for payment to another person for discharge in whole/part any debt or liability; III. Cheque has been presented to the bank within a period of six months from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of its validity whichever is earlier. RBI in its notification DBOD.AML BC.No.47/14.01.001/2011-12 has reduced the aforesaid period from 6 months to 3 months. IV. Returning of the cheque unpaid by the drawee bank for want of sufficient funds to the credit of the drawer or any arrangement with the banker to pay the sum covered by the cheque; V. Giving notice in writing to the drawer of the cheque within 30 days of the receipt of information by the payee from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid demanding payment of the cheque amount; VI. Failure of the drawer to make payment to the payee or the holder in due course of the cheque, of the amount covered by the cheque within 15 days of the receipt of the notice. The offence under Section 138 , NI Act is made out against the drawer of the cheque, only when all the aforementioned ingredients are fulfilled. CC No. 41970/2019 Varsha Khanna Versus M/s KSBL Securities Limited Page 7 of 15 Digitally signed by AASTHA SHARMA AASTHA Date: SHARMA 2026.07.10 16:47:04 +0530 11. Analysing all the concerned provisions of law and various pronouncements in this regard, the Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of Basalingappa v. Mudibasappa [AIR 2019 SC 1983] held that: I. Once the execution of cheque is admitted, Section 139 of the Act mandates that a presumption be drawn that the cheque in question was for the discharge of any debt or other liability. II. The presumption under Section 139 is a rebuttable presumption and the onus is on the accused to raise the probable defence. The standard of proof for rebutting the presumption is that of preponderance of probabilities. III. To rebut the presumption, it is open for the accused to rely on evidence led by him or the accused can also rely on the materials submitted by the complainant in order to raise a probable defence. Inference of preponderance of probabilities can be drawn not only from the materials brought on record by reference to the circumstances upon which they rely. IV. That it is not necessary for the accused to come in the witness box in support of his defence. Section 139 imposes an evidentiary burden and not a persuasive burden. It is therefore implied that the law regarding the presumption for the offence under Section 138 , NI Act, the presumptions under Section 118(a) and Section 139 have to be compulsorily raised as soon as the execution of cheque by the accused is admitted or proved by the complainant and thereafter the burden is shifted upon the accused to prove otherwise. CC No. 41970/2019 Varsha Khanna Versus M/s KSBL Securities Limited Page 8 of 15 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2026.07.10 16:47:08 +0530 Appreciation of evidence and marshalling of facts: 12. Issuance of cheque: The complainant has filed on record the original cheque, i.e. Ex. CW1/C. In notice under Section 251 CrPC, the accused has admitted that the cheque in dispute belongs to his company and his signatures on the same. It is also not disputed that the cheque in question is not drawn on the account maintained by the accused person and it is impliedly admitted therefore that the accused is the drawer of the cheque. Therefore, ingredient number I stands fulfilled in the present case. 13. Presentment and dishonor of cheque: As per the RBI guidelines, it is essential for the cheque in question be to presented within a period of three months from the date on which they are drawn and the same be returned as unpaid by the drawee bank for want of sufficient funds to the credit of the drawer or any arrangement with the banker to pay the sum covered by the cheque. In the case at hand, the cheque in question was returned vide return memo dated 29.08.2019 (Ex. CW1/D) due to the reason "Payment stopped by the drawer". By implication thereof, the cheque was presented within three months and the same was returned. Therefore, Ingredient number III & IV stand fulfilled in the present case. 14. Legal demand notice and payment by the accused thereof: The legal notice dated 25.09.2019 (Ex. CW1/E) was dispatched vide post (Ex. CW1/F (Colly)), i.e., within 30 days of return of the bank memo indicating cheques in question being unpaid. The fact that the legal demand notice has made a clear and unambiguous demand for payment of the cheque in question is not disputed. The accused has not accepted the receiving of legal demand notice in notice u/s 251 CrPC. However, as CC No. 41970/2019 Varsha Khanna Versus M/s KSBL Securities Limited Page 9 of 15 Digitally signed AASTHA by AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2026.07.10 16:47:12 +0530 per the presumption raised under Section 114 of Indian Evidence Act, 1872 and Section 27 of General Clauses Act, if the legal demand notice is sent at the correct address, then the same shall be deemed to have been duly served, as per the precedent laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in C.C. Alavi Haji v. Palapetty Muhammed , (2007) 3 SCC (Cri). The ingredient number V is fulfilled by virtue of giving legal demand notice within 30 days from the bank return memo. The receipt of legal demand notice by the accused is deemed to be admitted as per the discussion above. 15. Moving on, it is not disputed that the accused has not made the payment of the cheque amount within 15 days of the receipt of legal demand notice. Therefore, ingredient number VI also stands fulfilled in the present case. Presumption under Section 118A read with Section 139 , NI Act 16. The NI Act raises two presumptions in favour of the holder of the cheque, i.e., complainant; firstly, with regard to the issuance of cheque for consideration, as contained in Section 118(a) and secondly, with regard to the fact that the holder of cheque received the same for discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability, as contained in Section 139 of the Act. These presumptions shall end only when the contrary is proved by the accused, that is, the cheque was not issued for consideration and in discharge of any debt or liability etc. The Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in its judgment titled Rangappa Vs. Sri Mohan , (2010) 11 SCC 441 held that a reverse onus clause usually imposes an evidentiary burden and not a persuasive burden and when an accused has to rebut CC No. 41970/2019 Varsha Khanna Versus M/s KSBL Securities Limited Page 10 of 15 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2026.07.10 16:47:16 +0530 the presumption under Section 139 , the standard of proof for doing so is that of "preponderance of probabilities". Therefore, if the accused is able to raise a probable defence which creates doubts about the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability, the prosecution can fail. It was further held that the accused can rely on the materials submitted by the complainant in order to raise such a defence and it is conceivable that in some cases the accused may not need to adduce evidence of his/her own. Once a probable defence is raised, then the onus is shifted to the complainant to establish that a legally enforceable liability existed in his favour and the burden of proof on the complainant in this case is that of "beyond reasonable doubt." 17. The accused can rebut the presumption as raised under Section 138 , NI Act by: (a) putting forth his defence at the time of framing of notice u/s 251 CrPC; (b) cross-examining the complainant; (c) when statement of accused is recorded u/s 313 CrPC; (d) or by leading defence evidence, thereby demolishing the case of the complainant. Rebuttal of Presumption by Accused as to existence of legally enforceable debt 18. In light of the above discussion, since the accused has admitted to issuance of cheques, admitted the signatures on the cheque and legal notice has also been deemed to be served, what is left to be seen is whether the accused has been able to CC No. 41970/2019 Varsha Khanna Versus M/s KSBL Securities Limited Page 11 of 15 Digitally signed AASTHA by AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2026.07.10 16:47:20 +0530 rebut the presumption against him, i.e., whether the accused is able to raise a probable defence which creates doubts about the existence of a legally enforceable debt? 19. In the present case, in order to discharge his initial burden to prove the abovementioned ingredients, the complainant relied upon the affidavit of the complainant being Ex. CW1/1 and placed on record documents mentioned hereinbefore. 20. The primary defence of the accused person is that the complainant has misused the security cheques and that he does not owe any liability towards the complainant. The case of the complainant is based on Ex. CW1/A which is the MoU dated 10.07.2017. As per the MoU the complainant had invested Rs. 9,00,000/- with the accused company, the same is also admitted by the accused. The defence of the accused is that the amount invested by the complainant was subject to market risk and the accused company issued stop payment instructions to the bank when it suffered losses. The Ld. Counsel for the accused has argued that there is no legally enforceable debt as the impugned transaction is not a loan but trading investment; which is based on contingency/market fluctuations. It is clear from the Ex. CW1/A and the statement of accused number 2 as DW1 that 15% interest was to be given on excess deposit i.e. the amount which is not invested in the trading. The burden of proving the amount invested in trading was on the accused. The complainant has admitted receiving interest at the rate of 15% for some months. The burden was on the accused to show on what amount the interest was being advanced to the complainant; because if it was on the principal CC No. 41970/2019 Varsha Khanna Versus M/s KSBL Securities Limited Page 12 of 15 Digitally signed by AASTHA SHARMA AASTHA Date: SHARMA 2026.07.10 16:47:24 +0530 sum given by the complainant, that would have meant that the entire sum given by the complainant is being treated as excess deposit. The accused has not produced any evidence to show where the amount given by the complainant was invested and how much loss was suffered on the same. 21. The Ld. Counsel for the accused has argued that the complaint does not disclose the exact liability of the accused. This argument of the accused does not hold any ground; since the complainant has produced the MoU showing advancing of the cheque amount to the accused. The burden was on the accused to show that there does not exist any/part liability against the cheque in question. 22. The Ld. Counsel for the accused has further argued that the MoU is not an enforceable contract as the same is a wager agreement as the outcome depends on a future contingency and no return can be guaranteed in arbitrage activities. This argument of the accused is also flawed. Arbitrage contracts are enforceable, however, the amount claimed at the end may depend on the profit/loss on the amount invested. The complainant has clearly stated that she has received interest at the rate of 15% for some months. During the cross-examination of accused number 2 as DW2, when it was specifically asked what was the interest that was given to the complainant, he answered, "I do not remember if the accused no. 1 company had given return at interest as agreed per month to the complainant on principal amount. I do not remember if the accused no. 1 company used to return money alongwith interest to the complainant per month. (Vol. The account department would know.) CC No. 41970/2019 Varsha Khanna Versus M/s KSBL Securities Limited Page 13 of 15 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2026.07.10 16:47:29 +0530 From the statement of the accused, it can be deduced that he is unaware about the details of the amount invested in the market out of the principal sum given by the complainant. In the absence of any evidence, it is impossible to conclude what amount was treated as excess deposit on which the interest was being given to the complainant. Again, the burden of showing the same was on the accused, which he has failed to discharge. 23. The Ld. Counsel for the accused has also argued that the complainant has already received the claim from IRP and the proof of the same is Ex. DW1/4. The ingredients of the offence punishable under Section 138 of NI Act are clear. Only the amount which has been paid before the presentation of the cheque is material while determining the liability of the accused. Clearly, in the present case whatever amount the complainant has received is after the presentation of the cheque in question. 24. The accused number 2 in his cross examination as DW1 has admitted that he was managing day to day affairs of accused number 1 and his signatures on the cheque in question. The above admissions are sufficient to invoke vicarious liability of accused number 2 as per Section 141 of NI Act. 25. In the present case, the accused has failed to even create any doubt, let alone discharging his burden of proof to rebut the presumption u/s 138 , NI Act. The accused has neither brought any witness nor any documentary evidence on record to substantiate his claim. It is the duty of the accused to punch holes in the story of the complainant which he has not been able to do. On the other hand, the CC No. 41970/2019 Varsha Khanna Versus M/s KSBL Securities Limited Page 14 of 15 Digitally signed AASTHA by AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2026.07.10 16:47:32 +0530 complainant has brought documentary evidence to prove his version of the story along with the benefit of presumption u/s 139 , NI Act in his favour. 26. In light of the discussion above, ingredient no. II has been fulfilled in the present case. Conclusion: 27. In view of the evidence adduced, documents put forth and arguments advanced by the parties and further in view of the above discussion, the court is of the considered view that accused no. 2 Sh. Ramesh Arora is guilty of offence under Section 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 and accordingly, accused is hereby convicted under Section 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. 28. Copy of this judgment be given to the convict free of cost as per rules.
